We next come to the matter cf changing the names of the grades, which was pretty fully discussed in committee on a previous occasion. Two things are apparent-that the committee is not all agreed upon either one or the other names. The proposition I made was to eliminate ' Manitoba ' and substitute the words either ' Canada ' or ' Canada Western I have not particularly changed my views with reference to it. But I never like trouble in the family, and some of the younger members of the family are very tenacious of the old name. I do not like to inflict any unnecessary pain upon good members of the family by withdrawing from them a name which has been dear to them from their youth up. They seem to have been cradled on Manitoba wheat, brought up on Manitoba Hard or No. 1 Northern, and it has gone to the very root and fibre of their being. I am not so hard hearted as to try to pull it up. However, there is another consideration that has been presented to me that although it would not make much confusion in the matter of wheat. I am told by exporters of flour that to change the name from ' Manitoba ' might have a far-reaching effect in the matter of flour, it would not have so much effect in respect of wheat. The flour which is made from wheat is sold in countries to which it is exported under 'Manitoba* of different grades, and the fear has been expressed by large exporters of flour that some confusion and possibly loss might ensue if the names were changed. Under these considerations I think it would be just as well for us to leave the matter stand as at present.
In regard to all the different grades?
Yes, so far as wheat is concerned.

I hope the committee will pardon me for saying that I think this is a case where second thoughts are not the best. I think the committee came practically to a certain conclusion on the previous occasion. The committee accepted the minster's suggestion, but added somewhat to it; it was the suggestion, at any rate, upon which the majority of the committee would have agreed, I think. I would strongly urge that if there is any difficulty about changing these names

that difficulty will increase year after year, and not diminish. There is no doubt at all that the names at present are an anomaly I venture to express the opinion that the reason given by tbe exporters of flour has absolutelj no foundation. They are at liberty to call their flour by whatever name they please; as a matter of fact any change we would make in this Grain Act would net prevent them from doing so still. I cannot think that there is any warrant for their position in this matter. They would be, by all the laws of right and reason and morality, perfectly entitled to name their flour ' Manitoba ', although it was made from northwestern wheat, or wheat that carried the name ' Canada Western.' They would surely have just as much warrant in giving their flour the name * Manitoba ' as thev have to-day in giving their flour that name, although the wheat from which it is made never saw Manitoba. I pre same that is exactly what is done. We will suppose that flour ground at Moosejaw carries the name ' Manitoba ' but it never saw Manitoba. There is in that no moral wrong, that I know of. There is a certain quality expressed by the name, and that quality would be expressed by the same name just as well, though the wheat was marketed under a different name. I would urge this upon the minister, who I am sure takes a deep interest in this Bill, and I have no doubt he is taking a pardonable pride from his connection with it. But there are many others of us also who feel an interest in having legislation passed in such a shape that it would reflect credit upon us, and not condemn our judgment, not to say our common sense, if we allowed legislation to go through that, on the face of it, was not reasonable, and did not convey the idea that it purported to convey. Particularly is that the case now when we are submitting a new Act such as this, and under existing conditions it would be scarcely creditable to us if we did not. at as early a stage as possible, correct the anomaly that I have mentioned. We have no fault to find with those who in the first place gave these names to those grades, but conditions have changed since that time.

I would like to emphasize if possible the line of argument taken by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). Whatever difficulties exist now must become greater and greater each year as the proportion of wheat grown in Manitoba to the total wheat grown in the three prairie provinces, becomes less and less. I am sure the members for Manitoba will realize that we are not asking anything unreasonable. We are not asking for a name that will designate Saskatchewan as the producer of that wheat, or designate M. OLIVER.
Alberta as the producer; we are only asking for a name that will be as satisfactory tc Manitoba as to the other two provinces. Since this matter was up for discussion the other day I have had an opportunity of talking with a member of a large milling concern, and he says that if the change is made as proposed by the minister, that is, to bracket the former name, with that protection the millers cannot suffer any injustice. I am sure that if this name is not -changed at the present time, it will be a continual source of more or less irritation, it cannot be otherwise As the hon. member for Edmonton says, we are revising this Bill from one end to the other and we ought now to make this change, especially as we are not suggesting anything that anybody in Manitoba would have any good ground to object to.

Mr. Chairman, I spoke on this question the other day, and I said then that the wheat that was grown in southern Manitoba was the best wheat in the world. Som-e hon. gentleman took exception to that. I looked up the proof in the meantime -and I wish to give the evidence in connection with this matter. We had Dr. C. E. Saunders giving his evidence in the Agricultural Committee in 1910 and on that occasion he said:
By Mr. Sharpe (Lisgar):
Q. What reason do you give for the quality of wheat in Manitoba being better than the quality in other districts?-A. A m-ore favourable ripening season; warmer weathe)'.
Q. Superior to Saskatchewan?-A. Yes, I think, from my baking tests.
These were actual tests in baking.
Q. If you were a miller would you pay more for Manitoba wheat than Saskatchewan wheat? A. I think probably I should be willing to pay a little more especially in an unfavourable season, provided the Manitoba wheat was of the same grade and equally good in appearance.
Here we have the statement of the best qualified man we have in Canada, a man who has gone into this question fully and made actual tests by baking the flour, and ihis -evidence goes to show conclusively that the wheat coming from southern Manitoba is the best wheat gro-wn in the world to-day. As for this change that is proposed by my good friends from the west from * Manitoba ' to ' Western ' or ' Canada ' wheat, as far as ' Canada ' wheat is concerned, I do not think we should consider that for a moment, and as far as making it ' Western ' wheat is concerned, I do not think we should -consider that either, because, as I stated the other day, Manitoba was the first province to go into the growing of wheat in western Canada, and I think that Manitoba is entitled to have the name -of the wheat remain as it is.
Why has she any more right 'than the rest?

Because the
name is there and it is established all over the world. There is no reason for the change.
The hon. gentleman surely will not say that because a person has had a favour he is entitled to a continuance of that favour?

it is not a
favour at all; it is a name that is established all over the world, and why change it?.
We might let you keep it if you said it was a favour, but when you say that you have a right to it, that is different.

If the grain grown in southern Manitoba is the best that is grown, how does my hon. friend account for the fact that last year, when there was a prize given of $1,000 in cash for the best wheat, the wheat that won that prize was produced not in southern Manitoba and not in southern Saskatchewan, but in the more northern portion of the province of Saskatchewan. I have no doubt but that you can take samples of wheat from southern Manitoba, which -grows fine wheat- I cannot complain of the quality of wheat in southern Manitoba-compare that with wheat from some parts of Saskatchewan and the Manitoba wheat may be found to be better. But what I claim is that wheat on the average grown throughout southern Manitoba is not any better than wheat grown throughout southern Saskatchewan, because it is practically the same class of wheat, and I know as a matter of fact that the millers, who are better judges than

anybody else, keep their analysts there every day to test every car load of wheat having reference to where it comes from, and they say that the wheat of southern Saskatchewan is equal in every respect to wheat from any other part of the west. A great many portions of northern Saskatchewan also produce equally as good wheat for milling purposes; so that the claim that Manitoba wheat is better cannot be made good if you go to the men who buy wheat for grinding purposes and pay for it, because they pay just as much tor wheat grown west of Manitoba as they do for wheat grown in Manitoba.

The hon. gentleman asked me how I accounted loi wheat in Saskatchewan winning the thousand dollar prize. That brings us to the question of the grading of wheat m western Canada, and, in my humble opinion the grading of wheat in western Canada is on a wrong basis.	,
I consider that all wheat should be tested, and graded according to the test and that the system should not be as .it is at the present time. In the grading rooms in Winnipeg, you find a long table with hundreds of samples, and they will look at each sample and they will grade it according to its appearance as JNo. 1, No 2 and No. 3 and so on, while, as a matter of fact, if you would test each of these samples, as has been done in some cases, vou would very often find that No. 3 would make just as good flour, as No. 1 or No. 2. I consider that the system should be changed, and the wheat graded according to actual tests.

When the matter was considered before by the committee, I expressed myself in favour of the change proposed by the minister to call it ' Canada Wheat/ I still! hold the same opinion, . but I have strong objections to the proposition of my hon. friend from Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) because that name would make the distinction between one part of Canada and the other even more pronounced than the original name ' Manitoba.' I say this for fear I may be misunderstood. If the alternative is between calling it ' Canada West ' or ' Manitoba ' for my part I would prefer to make no change and all the more so because the name ' Manitoba ' has earned a distinction in the markets of the world for which the Province of Manitoba is entitled to credit.

When the question was before the committee at its last sitting, I took the position that the word ' Manitoba ' should rerhain. I am glad to know that the minister has repented and decided that he is not going to unduly interfere with the trade of Canada in the markets of the world by changing the name from ' Manitoba.' It is quite reasonable that our friends in Alberta and Saskatchewan should each stand up for the name which iconieerns his particular province, but I trust these hon. gentlemen will take a wider view of the question. Remember, that Canada has built up a large trade throughout the world on the word ' Manitoba ' not only in wheat but in flour.
We might in this respect, take a leaf out of the book of our American friends under whose system all the wheat grown in the hard wheat belt of the United States northwest is practically recognized on the markets of the world as ' Duluth.' The mills in Minneapolis and Duluth grind millions of bushels of Kansas wheat, but thev shin that flour out branded ' Minnesota,' and they do that because that name has earned a world-wide reputation. In the same way the word ' Manitoba ' on our wheat to-day is worth millions of dollars to the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta. These other provinces will gain nothing by changing that name. Manitoba has a reputation in the wheat -markets ot the world, and it is worth more to the -province of Saskatchewan than it is to the province of Manitoba, because Saskatchewan now produces more wheat than the older -province. The hon. gentleman from Lisgar (Mr. Sharpe) made reference to the methods of inspecting wheat which -he thought were wrong, and he gave as an instance that No. 3 wheat sometimes made better flour than No. 1, but he -did not tell the House that No. 3 did not make as much flour as No. 1, and in that respect the grading is not too^ far wrong. I am glad the minister has decided not to interfere with the trade and commerce of the country by changing the name of our wheat. The hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Turriff) told us of a conversation he had with one of the large millers who said to him that our trade would not suffer any if the name were changed. Well, I have had -conversations with large millers, and they expressed the opinion that if the government unduly interfered with the business of the country in attempting to change this name, there would be a great loss to the whole Dominion, and I fancy that the opinion of these millers has had something to do with the change of heart which the Minister of Trade and Commerce has experienced.
The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) stated that we had practically agreed at the last sitting of the committee that we should change the name.
No.
Well, the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) certainly did make that statement.
I have no recollection of having made it.
My recollection is that nearly every man who spoke on the opposite side of the House stated that we on this side were agreed, to change the name.
I want to say right here now that I absolve the hon. member (Mr. Staples) from having agreed, because I remember very distinctly his request for a different name.

That is just the point l want to come to, because I thought the hon. member (Mr. Oliver), hud me in his mind when he made that statement. 1 was very careful to say that in case of a change I would prefer the name ' Prairie,' and I agreed to that only on condition that the word ' Manitoba ' was to be changed at all. Of course, I would rather have the word ' Manitoba ' remain. The hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) who is a practical miller, has told r.s the' other millers in this country have stated to him that there would be a material commercial loss if we changed the name, and there is no doubt about that. I trust this committee will vote to retain the name ' Manitoba ' which has done so much to establish throughout the world the high quality of wheat we are able to grow in Canada.

We should consider the matter very carefully before we attempt to change this name. It is my opinion that whether you change it or not, the buyers on the markets of the world, who know the brand, will continue to call it ' Manitoba.' My advice is: let well enough alone.
Hear, bean

We are often told that there is a broad spirit throughout the west, but some of the representatives of the west are very provincial when they get ('own here. The people of the other provinces were glad to call their wheat ' Manitoba Wheat ' at one time, and that, name has made a reputation -well-deserved. Anybody who has experience of the markets of England, knows that there is great danger in changing a trade-mark, if that trademark has been satisfactory to the market, and that applies to wheat as it. does to anything else. I believe we should retain the name ' Manitoba Hard 1 until we find something better.
My hon. friend (Mr. Broder), has told us that no matter what name we apply to this wheat the millers will continue to call it by the present name.
The change of the name would lead to confusion.

I do not think so, then is no confusion when they grind Kansas
wheat and call it ' Duluth,' and the hon. member (Mr. Broder), has said that the millers give the name ' Manitoba ' to wheat that never saw Manitoba.
I did not mention a word about the millers.

There is one point that I want to submit to the committee to show the absolutfe unfairness and injustice of the use of the name 'Manitoba' as applied to wheat. The higher grades are called .Manitoba; the lower grades are not called Manitoba. So far then as the name goes as an advertisement, it is a notice to the world that the only high grade wheat is grown in Manitoba, and that wheat not of a high grade	comes from	other provinces.
That is an absolute injustice to the other	provinces. I produced here
the other day the market quotations in the Manitoba 'Free Press,' and in these quotations _ the word 'Manitoba' was not used, because it happened, the grades that would call for that name were not on the market. I would like it to be thoroughly understood that this is not a mere matter of whim or caprice; I should think it is a case in which a very serious and grave injustice is done to three-quarters of the prairie area at the demand of one-quarter. That is not legislation that should commend itself to this parliament.
Mr.HENDERSON. As I stated the other day, I am not a resident of any of the prairie provinces and, therefore, I am not prejudiced in favour of one or of the other. I can quite understand that Iron, members from Alberta and Saskatchewan may be prejudiced against the use of the name 'Manitoba.' The class of wheat and flour-branded as 'Manitoba' has attained a high name in the markets of the world. I simply regard this name 'Manitoba Hard' as a name for a certain kind of wheat and I do not think it has anything to do with the particular part of the country in which it is grown. I believe that the western country would lose heavily if the name is changed. I think that people in Great Britain, and even Ontario, where they ask for 'Manitoba Hard' and are sent wheat called by another name, will have their suspicions aroused and will not pay the high price for it they otherwise would. I am conservative enough to stick to the old name and I do not think it is going to injure any of the other provinces. On the contrary, I believe it will be for the general benefit of the Dominion. I am glad the Minister of Trade and Commerce Has decided to leave the matter where it was, where it is, and where I hope it will -emain. For example, Indian corn is -ailed Indian corn, no matter whether it 's grown in Japan, or in Asia, or in The 'rgpntine, and the giving it of the name Indian corn does not in any way injure

the corn grown in the states of the American union. Indian corn is simply the name of a certain grain, and so it is that 'Manitoba Hard' has come to be the name of a certain species of grain, irrespective of where it is grown. We should leave it as it is and not take any chances.
Amendment (Mr. Knowles) negatived.

been discussed, as the minister said, in the family; and I congratulate him on the fact that the family gathered in a good sized audience without any desertions. My hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) the other day spoke with considerable emphasis in favour of the word ' Canada;' and hoping that he has not had the same experience as my hon. friend from Souris of getting lame in his views, I am going to move:

With reference to the next schedule, that of flaxseed. That is, 51 is substituted instead of 53, the idea being that flaxseed dries out rapidly. Instead of 52 pounds substitute 50, for the same reason. Then the third paragraph will read in this way:	'No. 2 Manitoba Flaxseed,'
dropping out the word ' all ' beginning the clause. Then it will read:
No. 2 Manitoba flaxseed should he flaxseed which is immature, or musty, or which contains more than twenty-five per cent, of damaged seed, and is fit for warehousing, and testing not less than 47 pounds to the bushel of commercially pure seed.
AVould that mean that it all had to be commercially pure seed?
Yes, * it has to be commercially pure seed.
Would not my hon. friend make that name ' Canada Western ' ?
That is what I proposed.
Would not my hon. friend consent to make the name ' Canada Western ' the same as in the case of oats and barley? I think it would be better to have it uniform,

There is no objection. It is suggested that the first section should read as follows:	'No. 1
Northwestern Canada flaxseed.' Then the second one to read: 'No. 2 Canada Western flaxseed.' That makes it the same as oats except the first one.

I am informed that the whole of the exported product of northwestern Manitoba for one year is about one car load. There is no doubt that most of the flax grown in Manitoba is grown in southern Manitoba.
It has that name no matter where it is grown.

Well, my hon. friend is privileged to keep the name. I would like to ask the minister the reason for making the weight so far below the standard weight of flax as stated in section 58. the present standard is 53 pounds in the first case, 52 pounds in the second and 40 in the third, all of them, as my hon. friend will see, several pounds lower than the standard. The matter comes with particular force because with all other grains we adopt a standard for the higher qualities which is higher than the weight laid down in the Act and I am afraid it will be argued that our flax seed is inferior on account of the lighter weight allowed notwithstanding the fact that we claim it is higher. It is a matter that is more technical than my knowledge goes. I find that in the Minnesota grades in the United States the same disparity exists

On section 115: no grade; condemned; rejected; scoured grain,

the practice of the inspection, I will move that, and let it stand for. consideration.

On section 124.

There was an opinion expressed against the mixing of grain in hospital elevators, and I understand the suggestion was carried so far as to say that no good grain should be taken into these hospital elevators at all. If that were done, I am told that the existence of these hospital elevators would be jeopardized, as it would leave little chance for them doing any work in seasons when there is not much damaged grain. The hospital elevator has been in existence for some years and it has given added value to a great deal of grain that would be otherwise valueless. I am informed that the hospital elevator has been caried on in a satisfactory manner so far as our officials know.

I am aware of the difficulty *of preventing the mixing of good grain "with the treated grain, once it is allowed into an hospital elevator, but, at the same time, I would urge on the minister that it is desirable to declare in the Act that such mixing shall not take place and then we would have to trust to the administration of the commission to ensure that mixing did not take place.
The Act now expressly forbids any mixing of grain ir. an hospital elevator.
I do not think it is explicit in that.
Yes, it prohibits mixing in a terminal elevator, and a terminal elevator is interpreted to include an hospital elevator.

The restriction says that hospital elevators can only be at terminal points. I can conceive that there would be a possibility that an hospital elevator might be required at some other place. There is at present an agitation for the establishment of internal storage elevators and a concomitant of this is an hospital elevator. I believe the railways are regarding, with very considerable favour, the proposition to establish these internal storage elevators at different places. This past season has shown, as never before how it would have been profitable to have internal storage elevators to take grain away from the prairies to some railway centre where it could be stored and treated. If this plan were adoipted by the railways at their own expense-I am not leaving out for the present the question of the government financing such internal storage elevators-there would be a necessity for hospital elevators in connection with them. A gieat many prominent farmers in the west are of the opinion that this, question should be taken into serious consideration by the transportation companies and the government. _ If we had had such a system this year it would have meant the saving of millions of dollars to the farmers of the west. I would suggest that the restriction of confining hospital elevators to terminal points be omitted. Then again, the Minister of Trade and Commerce informed me some time ago that it was possible inspection might be arranged for at different internal places, calling them subdistricts within the inspection division. It is possible for the ib-oard, with or without the concurrence of the Governor in Council, to establish machinery, at points such as Saskatoon, Brandon and Moosejaw, for instance, without coming to parliament for further authority.

So far as it appears to me now, I see no reason in the world why an hospital elevator should not be at at any other place as well as at Fort William or Port Arthur. In any case, there is no reason why at say an important place like Calgary, which may have a large storage elevator, there should not be an hospital elevator. If internal storage elevators are to be established throughout the west, it would be of the Very greatest benefit that there should be hospital elevators in connection with them. While this sec-

tion would not permit it, and while I do not see any reason why it should not be done, I will not make any change without further consideration. As to whether the board has authority to establish complete inspection districts, within inspection divisions, and to equip them as order points and the like of 'that, I think my hon. friend will come to the conclusion, when he studies the question, that the lesser the number of these subdivisions the better for the general working of the Act. My information is that they should be extended Very conservatively and not without great public necessity.
Mr.-KNOWLES. Suppose in the town of Moosejaw an. internal storage elevator were to be constructed, and there would be an hospital elevator in connection with it, one of the advantages which is spoken of a.s being a strong one if that were done is, thai the farmers would toe able to get certificates showing the amount of grain they have there and the grading of it, and then be able to finance as .now, when they have it in the ordinary elevators. Would this Act give power for the appointment of such necessary government officials as would grade that wheat and give such a certificate, without coining back to parliament to get the Act changed?
Sections 18 and 20 give full power to the board and the Governor in Council to establish inspection divisions for the inspection of grain, and therefore for the granting of certificates.
That is satisfactory.

The minister has promised to consider the advisability of permitting other hospital elevators throughout the country. mse
factory generally. I am willing to admit that the late government did not do as much as they might have done, and perhaps were derelict in their duty in that respect, but they have been punished for their sins. Now that gentleman opposite are in office they have the power to give a remedy. Is there any hon. gentleman in this House who will defend the principle that the people of the western provinces should pay from fifty to one hundred, and in some cases one hundred and fifty per cent higher for the same service than is paid by the people of the east? Will any one defend that state, of things in face of the testimony of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company themselves that it costs very much less to operate the railways in the west than it does in the east. This is not a political matter; Liberal and Conservative alike have to pay the freight rates. The Mr. TURRIFF.
question is what remedy shall be applied, and in my judgment the best remedy is for this House to express the opinion that the time has come when the discrimination that exists against the west in the matter of freight rates shall be put an end to. The only thing that would justify that discrimination against the west would be if the cost of building railroads there and operating them were greater than in the east, but we have the testimony of the Canadian Pacific railway, as I have said, that the reverse is the case. I purpose to-night moving an amendment which is practically in the words of the resolution adopted by the Winnipeg Board of Trade, a body of business men largely interested in the welfare of the west, a body composed of men on both sides of politics, and that board has come to the conclusion that there should be no further discrimination against the west. I want to give credit, where credit is due, and I say here that a very large part of the information I purpose putting before the House to-night was obtained by me from the articles in the Manitoba ' Free Press ' on this subject. The particular editor of the Manitoba ' Free Press ' who had charge of this work, has done more in the last Year to help us to get a change in these freight rates than did the late government, or this government, or the Railway Commission, or any other body. I admit, with regret, that before the publication in the' Free Press ' I did not know one-tenth of the extent of the discrimination against the west, and I do not believe that the former government, or this government, ever realized it. The man in charge of that particular work for the Manitoba* Free Press ', has I say, done more to bring about a change in the existing conditions than all the rest of us in Canada put together. Why, if the Board of Railway Commissioners had appointed one man like this gentleman on the ' Free Press ' to do the work, they could get all the necessary information to enable them to take hold of the question and to deal with it- The chairman of the Railway Commission wrote to the Minister of Railways that no specific case has been brought to his attention, but if wrong-doing exists on the part of the railways, it is not necessary, and it ought not to be necessary, for some one to lay a specific complaint before that board.
The Board of Railway Commissioners is appointed for the express purpose of deaii'ng with these matters, and in the Act appointing them they are given special powers to act on their own initiative. For such a board to say that there was any amount of wrong-doing going on, but that nobody had brought it to their attention, is to my mind only begging the question. They are there for the purpose of finding it out, and they have or

should have a staff of experts to give them the necessary information. I do not '.rant to say anything in criticism of that board. As I have said in this House before, I believe its chairman is the best man for the position in the Dominion of Canada. There are other good men on the board. But they have been crowded with work, much of it of a trivial character. They have been kept busy by the railway companies on one pretext or another, so that they have not had time to give, or at least have not given, the attention that should have been given to the subject of freight rates.
If they have not had time, what are you censuring them for?

There are plenty of good men to be engaged. How did the Manitoba ' Free Press ' get all the information? I do not suppose that its chief editor had time either, but he had the common sense to hire a man who could get it.
Why didn't you have the common sense to advocate what you are doing now when you were on this side of the House six months ago?

I did go to the Rail. way Commissioners six months ago, and if I sat on the other side of the House, with my friends in power, I would have brought the matter up before this time, and just as strongly and earnestly as I am doing now. This is not a matter of party politics at all There is an injustice to be rectified, and our hon. friends opposite are in a position to be able to rectify it. We on this side of the House can only bring it to their notice. But I think my hon. friend the Minister of Customs wiil have enough to do if he rectifies everything that is wrong in his own department. He may have trouble enough on his hands without trying to take the -weight off the shoulders of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways, who, I am sure, is quite able to look after his own department, and will be quite willing, when he sees the extent of the injustice, to relieve the people of the west. In order that the Board of Railway Commissioners may be enabled to handle this work, I am satisfied that that board must either be enlarged in number or be given more money and more help. They are not able, with the help they now have, to handle properly the business that comes before them. This House for the last three or four years has been placing one thing and another on the shoulders of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and I think they bare more than they can do. My judgment is that the board should not be divided into an eastern and
a western section. I do not think that is necessary. I have no doubt there are injustices in the matter of freight rates existing in the east as well as in the west. My view is that or.e of these sections should deal solely with freight matters from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and that there should be on it representatives not merely of the east or -west but of both. If this parliament expects the board to do the best work that is possible, it must supply it with the necessary amount of money to enable it to engage the proper kind of staff, so that it may be able to attend to the business. Suppose it did cost $50,000 or $100,000 per annum more than it costs to-day to bring that board up to the point of efficiency, it would be the best spent money this House could vote. Why, if you take the extra rates that have been for years imposed on the people of the west over and above the rates charged in other parts of the country for the same services, you would not count it by hundreds of thousands, but by millions and tens of millions. We are not going, to argue that we in the west should be given cheaper freight rates than obtain in the east; but we think the time has come when the railways should not be allowed any longer to charge more in the west than in the east for the same service, unless they can prove that it costs them more to handle the business, which I am satisfied they cannot do, because they have already proven that it costs less. Some years ago a change was made in the passenger rates. Up to four or five years ago there were different rates charged all over the country. One branch of a railway would charge one rate, and another branch a short distance away would charge a higher rate. The matter was brought up in the House, and the rates were made equal from the Rocky Mountains to the Atlantic ocean-a flat rate of three cents a mile. If the railways can carry passengers at the same rate in the lower provinces, the centre provinces and the western provinces, why should they not cany a ton of freight at the same rate in the western provinces as they carry it in the eastern provinces?
Would it be inconvenient for the hon. member at this stage fo give us his amendment?

No. I will be most pleased to do that. It is as follows:-
Moved by Mr. Turriff, seconded by Mr. Martin: That in the opinion of this House the time has arrived when the government of the Dominion should, by legislation, lay down the principle that the rates to be charged by the railways in the western provinces shall not exceed those charged in Ontario and Quebec for a similar service, to a greater

extent than, necessary to cover any excess there may be in the cost of operation in the west over that in Ontario and Quebec.
As I stated in the beginning of my remarks, this resolution was adopted by the Winnipeg Board of Trade, practically in its entirety. Now, Mr. Speaker* I think it goes without saying that if we are to have anything like unity of feeling throughout this Dominion, if we are to have the good feeling that should exist between one end of the country and the other, you cannot possibly bring that about if the people at one end of Canada feel that every cay, from the first day of January to the last day of December, they are being deliberately robbed by the railway companies charging them from 50 to 150 per cent higher freight for the same service, that is given in eastern Canada. Nobody will say for a moment that the railways are not getting _ a good paying price for the freight they' are carrying in this part of the country. We had evidence of that when a strike occurred a year or two ago on the Grand Trunk railway in eastern Canada. That company refused, or objected, to pay the same rate of wages that was being paid by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. And what was their plea? That the Canadian Pacific railway had a large traffic in the west, where they got a very much higher rate of freight for the service rendered than either railway received here, and that the Grand Trunk, under those circumstances, could not really pay their men as high wages as the Canadian Pacific paid; but as soon as the railway to the west was completed, and they were able to get into that part of the country and obtain the high rates that the Canadian Pacific railway were then getting, they would be able to give their men better pay. I have not the slightest doubt that when the Grand Trunk Pacific railway is completed, that company will, if allowed, charge just as high rates of freight as the Canadian Pacific railway is getting now. And the Canadian Northern will do exactly the same thing. But it is for this House to say whether the time has come, or whether it has not, when we should lay down the principle that unless it costs the railway companies more to handle the freight and to build their lines, they should not be allowed to charge more in one part of the country than in another. We thought at one time than when the Canadian Northern commenced to operate in the west they would reduce the freight rates. Well the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific railway in some places run into the same town, from Winnipeg say, and thus we have the peculiar fact that in places where the two railways are operating the freight is higher for the same mileage in the Canadian Pacific railway. I have quoted figures to-night to show that the rates on the Canadian side of the boundary line are much higher than those on the American side.

Mr. Speaker, I trust that my hon. friend (Mr. Turriff), who has just taken his seat, will not consider me discourteous when I say that he cannot expect the hon. members of this House or the people of this country to treat any statement or resolution coming from him in regard to the freight rates that prevail in western Canada in any serious manner. If my hon. friend had a desire to be serious, there was a fitting time and place for it. He might have taken that course when the government that he supported sat to the right of the Speaker and had it in their power to remedy the condition of which he complains to-night. But, as has been shown, when this parliament was in session last year, the then Minister of Railways, and even my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) declared that the railway freight rates in western Canada were fair, just and reasonable to the people. Now my hon. friend undertakes by

his resolution to say that nothing but the cost, especially the cost of operation, must be considered. There is more than the cost of operation to be considered in determining the railway freight rates that are charged to the people of this country. We had an exhibition in this House yesterday which I am sure will long be rememberei by every hon. member who was present at the time, when my hon. friend the Minister of Railways laid upon the table a' statement that went to show that, as a result of the incompetency of the late Administration, we have a condition of affairs in the railway life of our country to-day which is most deplorable. I say more: We had presented to the people of this country through that official statement of the Department of Railways and Canals a state of affairs that goes to show not only the incompetence of the gentlemen who had in charge the government of this country, but a state of affairs that should make every member of that government and every gentleman who supported them in this parliament for the past 15 years hang their heads in shame before their fellow countrymen. If the hon. gentlemen who formed that Administration, and the hon. gentlemen1 who supported it, do not feel keenly enough their position to hang their heads in shame, I can tell them that there is not an intelligent citizen in this Dominion of Canada to-day who understands the railway situation and will study that statement as presented by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways, who will not blush with shame owing to the fact that we have had in the government of this country for the past eight or ten years men who are so utterly incompetent to discharge the public trust that has been reposed in them.
We had, Mr. Speaker, a statement to show that the eastern division was to cost us $250,000,000-I think that was the amount-and in addition we had the extraordinary statement-

Mr ROGERS If we are to have an intelligent understanding ox what our railway freight rates are to be, we must take into consideration the cost of construction, and not, as my hon friend (Mr Turriff) said, the cost of operating alone. And it is because of the necessity that arises for us to take into account the cost of construction that I am dealing with the figures I have just quoted. We have in addition the
extraordinary cost of the prairie section, and the very extraordinary cost of the mountain section which, in the case of the two, will amount to over $100,000,000. Therefore, we have, Mr. Speaker, a National Transcontinental railway being built, according to the latest statement, at a cost of something like $350,000,000 to the people of this country, instead of $15,000,000, as was stated. The right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), who now leads the opposition, appealed to this parliament (or its support and endorsation nine years t.go, pointing out, as he pointed out yesterday, that there was then necessity for the construction of such a railway, by reason of the fact that we had in western Canada great development in progress, and that need existed for a reduction in the railway freight rates in this country, and especially western Canada. He appealed for support in the first place in order that he might- be allowed to spend $13,000,000 to accomplish these results. His Finance Minister a few months later, discovering that a mistake had been made by the right hon. gentleman, rose in his place, and pre-si nted a supplementary statement showing that that railway should cost $51,000,000, instead of $13,000,000. And just a day or two ago the official figures were published, showing that the cost will actually amount to $350,000,000. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Turriff) has talked of the necessity -of reducing railway freight rates notwithstanding the conditions which his party have created, and with which we, as a new government. have to grapple at the ipresent time. Not only did the right hon. gentleman, at the lime, I speak of, appeal to this House for support and endorsati-on, but he went outside this parliament and appealed to Heaven in order that he might be protected in carrying out this great work, and in order that the railway freight rates should be reduced in the interests of the people. Sir, he was protected in respect to that ipolicy in the elections which followed, and he was similarly protected in the elections of 1908. But last year, when it was discovered that his humbugging policy was not productive of any good results to the country, a change took place, and not only Heaven, apparently, withdrew its support from him, but the great majority of the people in Canada withdrew their support, and relieved him of the high office which he held. Having those conditions to grapple with, nevertheless the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) rises in his place and declares that this parliament should at once dictate what the means of remedy should be. We have a Railway Commission of which we are all proud. We have vested in that commission all the powers necessarv to remedy the evils of which my hon. friend (Mr. Turriff) has

complained to-night He lias treated us to a dissertation by the hon. member (Mr. Turriff), but let me contrast it with a statement made about a year ago from his place in the House by the late Minister of Railways. Speaking on the 17th of January, 1911, Mr. Graham said:-
1 am not sure that they are so ready as that. However, the Railway Commission has complete control of rates in Canada. I agree with my hon. friend from South York, and I disagree with him. I believe that the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada is the best body, with the widest jurisdiction, of all such bodies in the world. I have had reason lately to make some investigation of this matter. In Germany, though the railways are government roads, the freight rates there do not compare for one moment with the rates in Canada. They are three times as high as our rates. Their hauls are short, it is true, but their rates should be low, because their cars are all loaded. France has not approached the control of rates as we have. England has a board, but in the control of freight rates it does not compare with the Interstate Commerce Commission or with ours, and the control exercised by the Interstate Commerce Commission does not for a moment equal with the control exercised by the Canadian Commission. Our commission can take anything they like as a basis for fixing the rates of the Canadian Pacific railway; they can take the dividend paid on the stock or the actual cost of the road, or they can have the company file a tariff, which will be as they see it a fair tariff for the transportation of freight and passengers. Let me call my hon. friend's attention to another point. I am not defending the Canadian Pacific railway. But if you take the rates in the United States-[DOT]

Being very much interested in this matter, it strikes me that whatever we are to do in this House, we ought to keep clearly in mind this fact, that we have established a board composed of able men. Now, Mr. Speaker, that is a statement made by the late Minister of Railways and Canals from his place in this House. What does the resolution of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), mean? We recognize on this side of the House the conditions in western Canada, not alone with regard to freight rates, but the deplorable conditions that exist in the prairie provinces, conditions for which the late administration are solely and entirely responsible. Now, Sir, recognizing that fact, having the most complete confidence in the Railway Commission, having asked them to take up and consider all complaints with regard to freight rates with a view of dealing with them in a fair and reasonable manner, not alone in western Canada, but throughout the Dominion, having also employed three of the ablest lawyers we could find to present the case of the people before the commission, then I say, having gone that far, it would be treating the commissioners, in whom we have the utmost confidence, with disrespect, it would be showing a lack of confidence in their judgment if we were to pass this resolution. Therefore, I take objection to this resolution on these grounds, and I ask hon. gentlemen on this side of the House to reject it, believing as we do, that it will serve no good purpose, inasmuch as this government have already taken the only legitimate course open to them of securing a remedy of the grievances of which the people complain, in the matter of railway freight rates..

I regret that I was not present to hear all the remarks of my hon. friend, but I take it that his remarks apply to one point, namely, the question whether this House should make a declaration as to the authority to be exercised by the Railway Commission over freight rates in western Canada. Regarding Mt. Lanigan's statement (page 61(12) that only 12 per cent of the grain crop moves under the rate complained of. The Northwest Grain Dealers' Association estimate of the 1911 grain crop in western Canada, is 304,207,500 bushels. 12 per cent of this would be 36,384,900 bushels, no inconsiderable amount.
Now, if my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) is under the impression that there is no local business doing in that western country, here are the facts given by the Winnipeg Board of Trade on the authority of Mr. Lanigan of the Canadian Pacific railway.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to assert that the whole 300,000,000 bushels moved, and that 12 pe- eent of it ought to move in this particular way?
The whole crop does not move,
Then, is it not cnly 12 per cent of what does move?
Yes, precisely.
Then give us what moves.
Instead of giving us the-figures given by the Board of Trade, suppose we cut them in two. I suppose that my hon. friend will admit that half the crop does move.
No.
Then I do not think I need srgue with my hon. friend any more.
I do not think anybody will admit that 160,000,060 bushels of the grain of the west does move.

Then my hon. friend and I do not agree, and I think he had better take his own opportunity of placing his views before the House. When he makes such a statement as that, I would not undertake to argue with him at ail. Suppose we say that only half the crop moves, then, according to Mr. Lanigan's calcuia-

lions, that 12 per cent is carried under local rates and these would affect the handling of 18,000,000 bushels of grain. Again I would say, with all due respect to this honourable House, that this is a matter of sufficient importance to take its attention for a few minutes.
Did the Railway Commission deal with that complaint?
This is a rejoinder to the defence made by the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian Northern railways to a con-plaint made by the Winnipeg Board of Trade.
Then it is all a part of a case before the Railway Commission -the complaint, the rejoinder and the reply. It is all before the commission still.

I cannot say what has become of it; but the expectation of the Winnipeg Boa/d of Trade, as expressed in the letters which have been read, was such that they believed that it was necessity to get an authoritative statement from this House as to what was required in the case. On the basis of the judgment given by the Railway Commission in the *express case, they did not expect substantial justice from the Railway Commission.
Did not the Railway Commission tell them in the early part of the proceedings that the law was ample and provided fully for dealing with the ease?
Certainly they did.
Then why should they want more law?

It is not that they ask that the commission should have more authority. The commission has authority, but it has not exercised that authority to remove this stupendous injustice, and the Board of Trade come to this honourable House and asks it to remove the injustice.
The commission is trying the ease.
Not at all, there is no ease to try.
The case is before the commission still.

It may, or may not, I cannot say, but I am taking the liberty of putting the case before this House, if I may, and it is of sufficient importance, both in matter and in principle, to warrant our attention. Speaking of the rejoinder of the railway companies, the Board of Trade says:
Mr. OLIVER,
A comparison 19 made of local mileage rates in Ontario, with rates from western points to Eort William. We submit that this comparison is unjust for the reason that a local mileage rate is compared with a terminal or proportional rate governing a part of a through haul, and necessarily the latter is much lower.
The board goes oil to say:
Regarding paragraphs 5 and 7 of Mr. Shaw's answer of October 12th wherein he contends that the price paid the farmer for his grain is based upon its expert value, and that, therefore, while a reduction in mileage grain rates would not increase the value of the grain to the farmer, it would needlessly reduce the railway's revenue. We contend that for the purpose of this investigation it is immaterial to the commission whether the producer or the consumer suffers as a result of the unduly high local mileage'grain rates. Of necessity it must he one or the other. However, as a matter of fact, the prices paid for feed grain are not m many cases based upon its export value but its value for feed in the locality to which it is consigned. However, in all cases, whether for feed or for export, the freight charges are deducted from the price paid for the grain in making settlement with the farmer. Therefore, the producer pays the freight charges.
The defendants contend that their local mileage grain rates between points in western Canada are reasonable because these rates compare favourably with rates shown in local mileage grain tariffs in the Dakotas and Montana. We submit that in so much 89 it is clearly shown in paragraph 9 of this letter that the local mileage tariffs in Dakota and Montana do not as a matter of practice govern the cost of moving grain and grain products between local points, for instance, between local points and such large centres of consumption a9 St. Paul and Minneapolis, and intermediate points to Duluth, Superior, etc., the unduly high rates charged for the movement of grain and its products between points west of Lake Superior cannot be justified by the comparison made by the defendants.
The defendants further contend that all privileges etc., connected with the milling of grain in eastern and western Canada must be considered in arriving at a reasonable rat** for the carriage of grain and its products between points west of Lake Superior, and endeavour to justify such rates by stating that different privileges are granted western millers than those extended to eastern millers. We submit that because a carrier applies different regulations for the milling of grain in transit is no reason or justification for charging unduly high rates on grain and letter, tlie same regtilations govern the milling of Manitoba grain in eastern Canada as in western Canada. Furthermore, in placing this argument before the commission, the carriers omitted to state that in eastern Canada special less than carload commodity rates are granted on grain products out from the mills, whereas in western Canada full class rates are exacted. We do not request, nor have we ever asked, that rates on grain and grain products between local jroints west of Lake Superior should be on as loir a basis as the terminal rates to Fort William and Port Arthur. These terminal, or proportional rates as they are specified in the tariffs, are simply one charge for part of a through journey, or in other words, part of a through irate, and those terminal rates, as has already been pointed out, were a matter of contract with the Manitoba and Dominion governments where the railways received value for the reductions made. We submit therefore, that it cannot be urged that because these terminal, or proportional, rates are low that local rates between points west of Lake Superior should be unduly high.
At the hearing in Montreal on July 23, 1911, our representative asked that local rates on grain and grain products between points west of Lake Superior should be reduced so as to show no greater difference over rates for similar service in eastern Canada than the 8th class maximum standard rates in western Canada shows over the 8tli class maximum standard in eastern Canada (grain and grain [DOT]products classify 8th class in carloads).
Since that time, however, copy of the evidence in the Vancouver rate case has been received, and the exhibit filed by the Canadian Pacific in that case shows a greater cost to move 1,000 tons of freight one mile in a portion of the territory where the eastern Canadian rates referred to in this answer apply, than in the territory west of Lake Superior where the rates complained of govern. We submit, therefore, that no higher rates
should be charged for the movement of grain and grain products between points west o' Lake Superior to the mountains than i charged on the eastern division of the Cana dian Pacific railway, where the cost of haulage is greater than in the former territory, and we would respectfully urge the commission to order that rates on grain and grain products handled under local mileage tariffs between points west of Lake Superior and the mountains should be reduced to an equivalent of those charged upon the eastern division, or, at least, that rates on grain and grain products handled under local mileage tariffs west of Lake Superior should not exceed the 8th class maximum standard rates in the western Canada by a greater percentage than the local mileage grain rates in eastern Canada exceed the Stli class maximum standard rates in eastern Canada.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have taken the liberty of placing before the House the statement of the Winnipeg Board of Trade in regard to this important matter. The board contends first, that the local rates on grain and grain products in western Canada are higher than the service rendered warrants. They are higher in proportion to tire rates charged for like service in eastern'Canada or in the United States, and they are higher in proportion to the rates charged by the same railway for carrying goods of the same class in western ' Canada than they are in eastern Canada. What they ask, and all they ask, is that the rates be placed on the same level, and made in the same proportion for the like service rendered, west of the lakes as east of the lakes. The conditions which exist in the prairie provinces at the present time makes it a question of more than ordinary importance. We have had the action of the government, taken _ in conjunction with the railway companies, for the purpose of securing the transportation and an outlet for the grain that is blockaded in the western provinces to-day, or a portion of it, to Duluth and Minneapolis. It is proposed to secure that outlet by a reduction in the rates Here is a condition which, according to the showing of the Board of Trade based on the figures given by the railway company, reduced again at the suggestion of my hon. friend from St. Antoine division of Montreal (Mr. Ames), which affects 12,000,000 bushels of that product in reaching its market.	.
It affects the transportation of 12 million bushels of the product, that to-day lies in the fields because it cannot reach the markets of consumers. If it was right *and reasonable that this government should take action with the railway companies, and take action with the United States Commerce Commission in order to secure a reduction of the rates to United States noints, surely it was just as right and reasonable that this government should take action witli our own Railway Com-nission to secure a reduction in the rates vithin our own country. To-day, because the grain cannot be transferred from the

field where it is produced to the local points of consumption, there is a burden on the transportation of that grain of from 40 to 90 per cent more than it should properly bear, according to the value of the service rendered, and the charges made for like service in other places, and on other lines, and even on the very same lines of railway.
Has not our government taken exactly the same action -with regard to our commission as the United States government have taken with regard to their commission?
Not as I understand it, and not as the Winnipeg Board of Trade understands it.
We are not responsible for their understanding.

If my bon. friend sized himself up with the Winnipeg Board of Trade, he would find that he did not have much advantage over them. They are generally reputed to be able to hold their own, intellectually or otherwise, with other people in this country, and perhaps to have some advantage. Now, is this a case of sufficient importance to warrant the consideration of parliament and of the government ? The contention of the Winnipeg Board of Trade, and the contention which I make, is that the case is of sufficient importance to warrant the consideration of this parliament and government. Then the question is, is this government and parliament to take no action, on the pretext that the matter is one for the Railway Commission and that they are entirely responsible for it? In my judgment on the case, as stated to the Minister of Railways by the Winnipeg Board of Trade, and from the fact that tile Railway Commission decided that a discrimination was proper between the east and the west in the matter of express rates, I think I have made out a strong case why this government should take immediate action in order to relieve the very undesirable conditions that exist in the 'west. This government and this parliament are responsible for the continuation of those conditions, and the people of the west will not cease earnestly to ask them to act without undue delay.
Does the hon. gentleman contend that the Railway Commission has not jurisdiction over rates in western Canada?

No, I said repeatedly that the Railway Commission has jurisdiction under the law. But in practice, the Railway Commission has not exercised that jurisdiction in order to bring about a general reduction in the rates such as the resolution asks for.

As I understand it, just as soon as the attention of the Minister of Railways was called to this matter he took up the question with the Railway Commission, and has been assured by them that they will immediately look into the freight rates in western Canada. The chairman of the board asserts that they have full jurisdiction over all rates, and will attend to the matter at once.

I wish to make my position clear in regard to this matter. We have in British Columbia, as the House is aware, a strong grievance, the same as.other sections in the west, and we have been fighting this question before the Railway Commission for a number of years. This week we closed a very long and technical argument on behalf of the Board of Trade of Vancouver before the commission. This whole question is going to be dealt with, and the initial steps were taken on Monday last. It seems to me therefore that the offering of this resolution is simply embarrassing the action of the board, that is, it is placing on the decision of the boardi which is not yet given, the condemnation of this House. We all acknowledge that this Board has been created for the purpose of dealing with just such matters as this, that the board has been constituted in such a way, that its personnel is of such a character as to make it very efficient. This board has done noble service for the people of Canada. Yet lion, gentlemen opposite are asking this government to condemn the board before they have had an opportunity of considering . the question. As I have said, the board have already taken the initial steps to deal with this question, and the present government have appointed counsel to look after the interests of the people on the prairies. I can assure hon. gentlemen that while the question, on the face of it, seems simple, it is one of the most intricate and difficult questions that can possibly be dealt with. Everybody who has had anything to do with traffic questions knows that railway traffic rates, the equalization and adjusting of those rates, is one of the most intricate questions that come before the Railway Commission. * I have taken a deep interest in this matter for a number of years, and I think it would be exceedingly unwise to bring this question to a vote. Hon. gentlemen themselves will acknowledge that this is a political move pure and simple. I will go this far with them, I will agree to a large extent with the statements made by the hon. member for Edimonton (Mr. Oliver), and with the statements made by the Winnipeg Board of Trade. I myself have a mass of figures to substantiate those statements, to a large extent. But what is the use of making arguments of this

kind to the House, and condemning the Railway Commission who are pursuing the only course that they can -pursue? If we take action of that kind, we should logically follow it up by abolishing the Railway Commission, and I do not think that even hon. gentlemen opposite are prepared to do that. As I understood it, the Winnipeg Board of Trade is objecting, apparently, to the decision of the commission on express rates. I have not gone through the whole evidence and argument but I venture to say, from the experience I have had, that the board must have had good, sound reasons for the decision they have given. We in British Columbia suffer a great deal more than they do on the prairies, that is the percentage is increased as you go west.	.
Hear, hear.

But I do feel that we should leave it to the Board of Railway Commissioners to deal with, give them all the assistance we can; I think it is well to air these things once in a while in the House, but I feel that to adopt a resolution of this kind, which must be construed as one of want of confidence in the commission, is inadvisable. The hon. member who moved the amendment (Mr. Turriff), has had the opportunity of getting this mass of information on ' Hansard ' and he might withdraw the motion. I feel that to adopt his amendment, would be to cast a reflection on one of the finest institutions we have in Canada.

MeKAY (Prince Albert). Mr. Speaker, before making a few remarks on this motion, I would ask the hon. member for Edmonton, if, when the question of express rates was brought before the Railway Commission, the public was represented by counsel?
I could not say.

While I am not in favour of the rates that now prevail in the west, I must say that I cannot supiport the amendment for the following reasons among others:	The trend of the remarks that
have been made by opposition members, who have spoken to this amendment, is. that although the Railway Commission had jurisdiction to deal with this matter, they remained passive, and in a decision given in a previous case somewhat analogous to this, that of the express Tates, the board did not follow the principle which hop. gentlemen endeavour to lay down in this amendment. Consequently, hon. gentlemen fear that in this other case, which is now before the Railway Commission a similar decision may be given.
Hear, hear.

The hon. members who have spoken, are seriously endeavouring
to redress the grievances that prevail in the west, and I am with them in the statement that such grievances exist with regard to railway rates, but I would remind them that in a case now before the Railway Commission with reference to freight rates, the present government has taken hold of that matter, placed it before the Railway Commission and employed counsel to watch the interests of the public.
In connection with the express rate investigation, counsel was employed to represent the public.

Even admitting that, the hon. member who moved this motion, himself admitted that on a previous occasion, when he made a speech in this House, he was not in possession of facts with which he is now familiar, and I presume that as these facts had not then become public property, the gentlemen who were conducting the case with regard to express rates, were not in possession of facts of which hon. gent-1 imen and the country at large are now in possession. I submit that the principle which it is endeavoured to lay down in this House, will be followed by the Railway Commission as the facts are now before the members of the Railway Commission and the counsel who will conduct the case for the public. I cannot conceive why that principle should not be followed to a great extent by the Railway Commission when it deals with this case, because it is a just and proper principle. I am against the amendment, for the reason that the Railway Commission now has this case in hand, it is in possession of the facts, and will deal with them in a proper manner. If the case is not dealt with in a proper manner, why then it can be dealt with by this House so as to afford the west relief from the grievances under which they are now suffering.
Amendment (Mr. Turriff) negatived or>
division.
Motion agreed to and House went into Committee of Supply.
There are two votes at ipage 62, which I wish to dispose of.
We have done a good day's work, and I hope my hon. friend will not insist on going on to-night.

There remain only one or two resolutions, and I have been bringing the officers -of my department up here for a Meek. I am anxious to complete the preparation of the supplementary estimates, but that cannot be done until these items are disposed of.
I understand the hon. the member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), has something to say.

I have postponed them twice already. I do not think the hon. member fox St. John can have any objection to these two resolutions which are yearly votes, for the lighting and heating, etc., of I'ideal! Hall, and public buildings.

I certainly do not wish to delay the passage of the estimates, but the votes that my hon. friend speaks of relate particularly to the city of Ottawa, and I would like to give my hon. friend the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy), who is partly representing the city of Ottawa, an opportunity to be heard when the votes are being considered. If my hon. friend will amicably consent to allow these items to stand until to-morrow, so that the hon. member for Russell can be here, I would be very glad, and if the member for Russell is not here I will promise that I will withdraw all objection to the items going through.

I do not like to be disobliging, although it seems to me that I have been as patient as possible. If it is desired that the hon. member for Russell should be here when we discuss these items having reference to the city of Ottawa, I will consent to what my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) proposes. There remains one item with reference to harbours and rivers in Prince Edward Island which we might pass and then adjourn.
Harbours, rivers -and bridges-generally- repairs and improvements, $10,000.
I do not think that the hon. gentleman is fair at this hour of the evening in asking us to take up this item, and I would strongly object to passing any more estimates.
I proposed that we should dispose of that item and then leave the items for Ottawa.

I have to ask the minister for some information in regard to this matter. I find that a number of items that were in the estimates passed last year and submitted by the late government have been dropped, particularly in regard to the county I represent. More than fifty per cent of the amount that was voted last year for harbours and rivers in Prince Edward Island has been left out of the estimates this year, and I would ask the minister if he could tell me the reason why.

The main estimates for Prince Edward Island were prepared in a hurry. Parliament was assembling a very short time after the new government took office, and it is intended to restore many of those items in the supplementary estimates. I can give that assurance to my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) right now.
There are some things I would like to point out to the minister before he prepares the estimates.
Would it not be more convenient for my hon. friend to give me a list of the works that he proposes?

I wrote to the minister giving him a list and asking him if he would give me an interview at any time and place that would suit himself and I would be glad to go over the items with him and point out the reason why I thought they should be put in the supplementary estimates. The minister answered my letter, but he did not reply to that request.
I will be glad to meet my hon. friend at any time.
If the minister would give me that privilege I will meet him in his office at an early date.

Yes, certainly, any time that will suit my hon. friend.
